items.stem: Which geophysical hazard is generally the most predictable in timing?
items.answer: Volcanic eruptions at monitored volcanoes
items.markingKey: Volcanic eruptions at monitored volcanoes. Precursors such as tremors, ground swelling and gas emissions often precede eruptions.

items.stem: Explain how speed of onset influences the impacts of geophysical hazards.
items.answer: Rapid-onset hazards such as earthquakes and landslides give little or no warning time to evacuate, so deaths are often high; slower onset allows warnings and evacuation, e.g. Pinatubo 1991.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rapid-onset hazards such as earthquakes and landslides give little or no warning time to evacuate, so deaths are often high; slower onset allows warnings and evacuation, e.g. Pinatubo 1991. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Small earthquakes release pressure and prevent large ones." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Small earthquakes release only a tiny fraction of the energy of large ones (each unit of Mw is about 32 times more energy).
items.markingKey: Small earthquakes release only a tiny fraction of the energy of large ones (each unit of Mw is about 32 times more energy). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Suggest why the Cascadia subduction zone is a concern even though no great earthquake has occurred there since 1700.
items.answer: Strain is accumulating on a locked megathrust; geological evidence shows Mw 9 events roughly every 300-500 years; a long gap means stored energy, not safety.
items.markingKey: Strain is accumulating on a locked megathrust; geological evidence shows Mw 9 events roughly every 300-500 years; a long gap means stored energy, not safety.

Calculate the annual probability of such an eruption.
items.markingKey: 1/24.2 × 100 = 4.1% Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that hazard magnitude is more important than frequency in determining hazard risk?
items.answer: Both matter: rare high-magnitude events dominate losses, but frequency shapes preparedness and long-term costs.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: high-magnitude events cause most deaths and losses (Tōhoku, Sumatra); they exceed the capacity of defences. Against / limitations: frequent small events cause cumulative damage and losses; frequency affects preparedness and perception. A supported conclusion might be: Both matter: rare high-magnitude events dominate losses, but frequency shapes preparedness and long-term costs. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "hazard magnitude"?
options: A series of long-wavelength ocean waves caused by the sudden displacement of water, usually by a sub-sea earthquake
The average time between events of a given magnitude, calculated as (n + 1)/m from a ranked record
A volcanic mudflow of ash, rock and water, often from melted snow and ice or heavy rain, which flows along river valleys
The size or energy of a hazard event, measured for example by Mw for earthquakes or VEI for eruptions
items.answer: The size or energy of a hazard event, measured for example by Mw for earthquakes or VEI for eruptions
items.markingKey: D. "hazard magnitude" is the size or energy of a hazard event, measured for example by Mw for earthquakes or VEI for eruptions.

items.stem: Distinguish between frequency and magnitude.
items.answer: Magnitude is the size or energy of a single event; frequency is how often events of a given size occur - the two are inversely related.
items.markingKey: Magnitude is the size or energy of a single event; frequency is how often events of a given size occur - the two are inversely related. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Maya writes: "A 1-in-100-year earthquake will not happen again for 100 years." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Recurrence intervals are averages; the probability of such an event is about 1% in any year, regardless of when the last one occurred.
items.markingKey: Recurrence intervals are averages; the probability of such an event is about 1% in any year, regardless of when the last one occurred. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: primary hazard

items.stem: Explain how a volcanic eruption can generate a lahar.
items.answer: Heat from the eruption melts snow and glacier ice, or heavy rain falls on loose ash; the water mixes with tephra to form a dense slurry that flows down valleys at high speed, as at Nevado del Ruiz in 1985.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Heat from the eruption melts snow and glacier ice, or heavy rain falls on loose ash; the water mixes with tephra to form a dense slurry that flows down valleys at high speed, as at Nevado del Ruiz in 1985. items.stem: Explain the difference between secondary hazards and primary hazards.
items.answer: Primary hazards come directly from the event (shaking, lava, ash fall); secondary hazards are triggered by it (tsunami, lahars, landslides, liquefaction, fires).
items.markingKey: Primary hazards come directly from the event (shaking, lava, ash fall); secondary hazards are triggered by it (tsunami, lahars, landslides, liquefaction, fires). items.stem: Using a named example, explain how secondary hazards increased the impacts of an earthquake.
items.answer: e.g. Tōhoku 2011: the Mw 9.1 earthquake generated a tsunami up to about 40 m high that overtopped sea walls, killing most of the roughly 18,500 victims, and caused the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear meltdowns.
items.markingKey: e.g. Tōhoku 2011: the Mw 9.1 earthquake generated a tsunami up to about 40 m high that overtopped sea walls, killing most of the roughly 18,500 victims, and caused the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear meltdowns.

items.stem: The 2015 Gorkha earthquake (Mw 7.8) caused about 9,000 deaths in Nepal (national population about 28.0 million); the 1995 Kobe earthquake (Mw 6.9) caused about 6,434 deaths in Japan (population about 125 million). items.answer: Nepal: 321.4 per million; Japan: 51.5 per million; higher: the 2015 Gorkha earthquake (Mw 7.8); e.g. building codes and enforcement, poverty and informal construction, preparedness and warning systems, governance and emergency response, depth/distance of the earthquake from population.
items.markingKey: M1 deaths ÷ population (millions); A1 321.4; A1 51.5. R1 R1 two valid, developed reasons.

items.stem: Using the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami, Japan as an example, explain tsunamis as secondary hazards.
items.answer: Waves up to about 40 m high overtopped sea walls and killed most of the roughly 18,500 victims. The tsunami caused far more deaths than the ground shaking.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that tsunamis are the most destructive geophysical hazard.
items.answer: Tsunamis are among the most destructive, but shaking causes more deaths over time.
items.markingKey: For: ocean-wide extent and high death tolls (2004). Against: infrequent compared with earthquake shaking. items.answer: It depends on the event: secondary hazards dominate for coastal and ice-capped settings, primary shaking for inland urban earthquakes.

items.stem: Explain why liquefaction occurs during earthquakes.
items.answer: Shaking increases pore-water pressure in saturated, loose sand and silt; grains lose contact so the sediment loses strength and behaves like a liquid, causing buildings to sink or tilt and sand boils to form.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Shaking increases pore-water pressure in saturated, loose sand and silt; grains lose contact so the sediment loses strength and behaves like a liquid, causing buildings to sink or tilt and sand boils to form. items.stem: A student claims: "The sea always rises first when a tsunami arrives." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Often the sea first withdraws (drawdown) when a wave trough arrives first, which can draw people onto the exposed seabed.
items.markingKey: Often the sea first withdraws (drawdown) when a wave trough arrives first, which can draw people onto the exposed seabed. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: concentrates more people and buildings in exposed locations

items.stem: Distinguish between formal housing and informal housing.
items.answer: Formal housing is planned, legally built and inspected under building codes; informal housing is self-built without permission or inspection, often on hazardous land and with weak materials.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Map description: a hazard map of a volcano shows lahar paths along three river valleys; two towns lie on the valley floors 20-50 km downstream; a third town lies on a ridge.

(a) Identify which settlements are most at risk from lahars. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest one land-use planning measure to reduce risk. [6]
items.answer: (a) The two towns on the valley floors, because lahars are channelled along river valleys. (b) Zoning to prevent new building on valley floors and relocating key services to higher ground, with evacuation routes to the ridge.
items.markingKey: (a) The two towns on the valley floors, because lahars are channelled along river valleys. (b) Zoning to prevent new building on valley floors and relocating key services to higher ground, with evacuation routes to the ridge. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: Examine the view that secondary hazards are more dangerous than primary hazards.
items.answer: It depends on the event: secondary hazards dominate for coastal and ice-capped settings, primary shaking for inland urban earthquakes.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: tsunamis caused most deaths in 2004 and 2011; lahars killed 23,000 at Armero. Against / limitations: ground shaking and building collapse caused most deaths in Haiti 2010 and Türkiye 2023; pyroclastic flows are primary and extremely deadly. A supported conclusion might be: It depends on the event: secondary hazards dominate for coastal and ice-capped settings, primary shaking for inland urban earthquakes. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: number of earthquakes per year worldwide (USGS averages) - Mw 8+: 1; Mw 7-7.9: 15; Mw 6-6.9: 134; Mw 5-5.9: 1,319.

(a) Calculate how many times more frequent Mw 5-5.9 earthquakes are than Mw 7-7.9 earthquakes. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, describe the magnitude-frequency relationship shown. [6]
items.answer: (a) 1,319 / 15 = 88 times (b) An inverse relationship: each one-unit increase in magnitude is roughly ten times less frequent.
items.markingKey: (a) 1,319 / 15 = 88 times (b) An inverse relationship: each one-unit increase in magnitude is roughly ten times less frequent. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "liquefaction".
items.answer: The loss of strength of saturated, loose sediments during shaking so that they behave like a liquid
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the loss of strength of saturated, loose sediments during shaking so that they behave like a liquid. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "hazard magnitude".
items.answer: The size or energy of a hazard event, measured for example by Mw for earthquakes or VEI for eruptions
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the size or energy of a hazard event, measured for example by Mw for earthquakes or VEI for eruptions. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "land-use planning".
items.answer: The regulation of where and how different activities may be developed in order to reduce exposure to hazards
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the regulation of where and how different activities may be developed in order to reduce exposure to hazards. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Felix writes: "Lahars only occur during eruptions." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Rain can remobilise ash deposits for years afterwards, as happened around Pinatubo for over a decade.
items.markingKey: Rain can remobilise ash deposits for years afterwards, as happened around Pinatubo for over a decade. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a forecast and a prediction.
items.answer: A forecast gives the probability of an event over a period and area (e.g. 30-year earthquake probabilities); a prediction states the specific time, place and size, which is not yet possible for earthquakes.
items.markingKey: A forecast gives the probability of an event over a period and area (e.g. 30-year earthquake probabilities); a prediction states the specific time, place and size, which is not yet possible for earthquakes. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how land use can increase the risk from volcanic hazards.
items.answer: Fertile volcanic soils attract farming and settlement close to volcanoes; towns built on valley floors lie on lahar paths; tourism brings visitors close to vents (Whakaari/White Island 2019).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fertile volcanic soils attract farming and settlement close to volcanoes; towns built on valley floors lie on lahar paths; tourism brings visitors close to vents (Whakaari/White Island 2019). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a lahar and a pyroclastic flow.
items.answer: A pyroclastic flow is a hot current of gas and fragments that moves extremely fast during an eruption; a lahar is a cooler mudflow of water and debris that follows valleys and can occur during or long after an eruption.
items.markingKey: A pyroclastic flow is a hot current of gas and fragments that moves extremely fast during an eruption; a lahar is a cooler mudflow of water and debris that follows valleys and can occur during or long after an eruption. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "All geophysical hazards are rapid-onset events." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Some volcanic eruptions build over weeks or months and some landslides creep slowly before failing.
items.markingKey: Some volcanic eruptions build over weeks or months and some landslides creep slowly before failing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Earthquakes kill people directly." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Most deaths are caused by collapsing buildings and secondary hazards, not by ground shaking itself - "earthquakes don't kill people, buildings do".
items.markingKey: Most deaths are caused by collapsing buildings and secondary hazards, not by ground shaking itself - "earthquakes don't kill people, buildings do". 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes (Mw 7.8 and 7.5) caused about 53,500 deaths in Türkiye (national population about 85 million); the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake (Mw 6.8) caused about 2,960 deaths in Morocco (population about 37.0 million). Calculate deaths per million people for each event.
items.answer: Türkiye: 629.4 per million; Morocco: 80.0 per million; higher: the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes (Mw 7.8 and 7.5)
items.markingKey: M1 deaths ÷ population (millions); A1 629.4; A1 80.0.

items.stem: A planner scores two places from 1 (low) to 10 (high) - a district of Kathmandu: hazard 5, vulnerability 2, capacity 8; a town near Mount Merapi: hazard 8, vulnerability 4, capacity 3. Using risk = hazard × vulnerability / capacity, calculate the risk score for each place and state which has the greater risk. Suggest how the place with greater risk could reduce it, other than by changing the hazard.
items.answer: a district of Kathmandu: 1.2; a town near Mount Merapi: 10.7; greater risk: a town near Mount Merapi; reduce vulnerability (building codes, land-use zoning) or increase capacity (warnings, drills, emergency services, insurance).
items.markingKey: A1 1.2; A1 10.7; R1 comparison. R1 strategy targeting vulnerability or capacity.

items.stem:
Study the resource below.

Table: deaths by cause, 2011 Tōhoku disaster (approximate) - drowning 90%; crushing and injury 4%; burns 1%; other/unknown 5%; total about 18,500 dead and missing.

Calculate the approximate number of deaths caused by drowning.
items.markingKey: 90% of 18,500 = 16,650 Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: USGS data: the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake, Morocco - Mw 6.8; the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake, Italy - Mw 6.3. Calculate how many times more energy was released by the first earthquake (energy increases by a factor of about 10^1.5 ≈ 31.6 per unit of magnitude).
items.answer: Energy ratio = 10^(1.5 × 0.5) ≈ 6 times

items.stem: With reference to the 2011 Tōhoku tsunami, Japan, explain how it illustrates tsunamis as secondary hazards.
items.answer: Waves up to about 40 m high overtopped sea walls and killed most of the roughly 18,500 victims. The tsunami caused far more deaths than the ground shaking.
items.markingKey: Context (Waves up to about 40 m high overtopped sea walls and killed most of the roughly 18,500 victims.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The tsunami caused far more deaths than the ground shaking. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to tsunamis as secondary hazards.

items.stem: Examine the view that geophysical hazards will never be accurately predicted.
items.answer: Eruptions are partly predictable; earthquakes can be forecast probabilistically but not predicted.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: no reliable short-term earthquake precursors; complex non-linear systems. Against / limitations: volcanic eruptions are increasingly forecast (Pinatubo); early-warning systems give seconds to minutes of warning. A supported conclusion might be: Eruptions are partly predictable; earthquakes can be forecast probabilistically but not predicted. items.stem: Examine the view that rapid urbanisation is the greatest cause of rising geophysical hazard risk.
items.answer: Urbanisation increases exposure, but whether it raises risk depends on governance and building standards.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: more people in megacities on faults; informal settlement on unstable slopes. Against / limitations: poverty, governance and corruption also matter; urbanisation can bring better buildings and services. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Data: a tsunami travels across ocean 4,000 m deep. Use v = √(gd) with g = 9.8 m/s².

(a) Calculate the speed of the tsunami in km/h. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain why this speed matters for warning systems. [6]
items.answer: (a) v = √(9.8 × 4,000) = 198 m/s ≈ 713 km/h (b) At about 700 km/h a tsunami crosses an ocean in hours, so warnings must be issued within minutes for nearby coasts but allow time for distant coasts to evacuate.

Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b).
